1.h4.name: Kádas Opening
1.h4.background: Also called the Desprez Opening, after the French player Marcel Després; Kádas is the name chess sites use today. Among the rarest first moves. David Bronstein liked to tell of a Russian player who always opened with 1.h4 and always won.

1.h4 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, which makes the rook trip to h3 a blunder at once: the bishop simply takes it. White's flank move has done nothing for the centre, so Black can take space there and enjoy a comfortable game.

1.h4 e5.strategy: Claims the centre and frees the queen and the dark-squared bishop at once. White's h-pawn has done nothing against it, so Black stands comfortably; the pawn on e5 is the target White will challenge first.

1.h4 a5.name: Kádas Opening: Koola-Koola Variation
1.h4 a5.strategy: Answers a flank move with a flank move. Black spends a tempo on a pawn that does nothing for the centre or for development, so the balance is kept but nothing is gained, and the fight for the centre starts only now. Harmless rather than ambitious.

1.h4 c5.strategy: Fights for the d4 square from the wing and keeps the e-pawn free, a sound way to ignore White's odd first move. It does not claim the centre outright, though, and invites White to throw in a wing pawn to deflect the c-pawn.

1.h4 f5.strategy: Controls the e4 square from the flank without occupying the centre. It is sound enough, but it loosens Black's own kingside and the diagonal toward the king, which White can try to use at once.

1.h4 g5.name: Kádas Opening: Schneider Gambit
1.h4 g5.strategy: Offers a wing pawn for nothing: White simply takes it and is a clean pawn up, with the rook on h1 freed. Black's own kingside is loosened and there is no compensation, which makes this an unsound gambit.

1.h4 c5 2.b4.name: Kádas Opening: Kádas Gambit
1.h4 c5 2.b4.strategy: A wing gambit: White offers the b-pawn to pull Black's c-pawn away from the centre and gain space there. It costs a pawn and a second flank pawn move for a modest lead, and Black can just take the pawn and develop.

1.h4 c5 2.Nf3.strategy: Brings a piece out and eyes d4 and e5, the squares Black's c-pawn is meant to contest. White carries on with ordinary development and treats the h-pawn move as a spare flank step, though it makes castling short a little less attractive.

1.h4 c5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and invites a fight of the Sicilian type in which White has the extra h-pawn move. That move does nothing for development, so Black is a little ahead in the race and White has to play energetically.

1.h4 d5 2.d4.strategy: The principled reply: White claims the centre with a pawn and goes for a solid queen's pawn game in which the h-pawn move is just an extra flank step. The position is the same as when the pawn moves are played in the other order.

1.h4 d5 2.Rh3.name: Kádas Opening: Beginner's Trap
1.h4 d5 2.Rh3.strategy: Loses material: the c8-bishop, freed by ...d5, takes the rook, and White can only recapture with the g-pawn. White is down the exchange, with doubled h-pawns and a damaged kingside, for nothing in return.

1.h4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Brings the knight out to control the centre from a distance instead of occupying it with a pawn at once. It keeps the pawn structure flexible and can still lead to the same queen's pawn positions, with White's development a step ahead.

1.h4 e5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 straight away to open the centre. Black can simply take the pawn, so White must back the idea with further sacrifice or quick development, and the early h-pawn move leaves White a little behind in the race.

1.h4 e5 2.g3.strategy: A sober reply: the g-pawn prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop on the long diagonal and keeps the kingside closed, so the advanced h-pawn does not leave White's structure in pieces. White builds the centre slowly and accepts a quiet game rather than a gamble.

1.h4 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the e5 pawn, but Black's pawn advances with a gain of time: the knight has to move again at once, and Black takes space for free. White still finds a good central square for the knight, so the move is playable but not ambitious.

1.h4 e5 2.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes White's central pawn, leaving Black a pawn up with the more natural development. The extra pawn is worth keeping, but White gets time to build lines, so Black has to go on developing with care.

1.h4 e5 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops and defends e5, a sound way to decline the pawn. But White gains space at once: the pawn advance to d5 hits the knight, which must retreat, and Black has not collected the pawn on offer.

1.h4 e5 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops, but lets White take on e5 for nothing in return. Black wins the pawn back with the knight only after White has built a big centre with tempo, and White stands clearly better.

1.h4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3.name: Kádas Opening: Kádas Gambit
1.h4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to open lines for the pieces. If Black takes again, White is two pawns down for a lead in development, and that is hard to justify when the h-pawn move has already cost a tempo.

1.h4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with the queen in the centre, so material is level. Black can chase the queen with a developing move and gain time, which is the price, but White is no longer a pawn down and the game is sound.

1.h4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and aims to win the d4 pawn back with the knight while the queen stays at home. Black can defend it, so White may remain a pawn down, but the pieces come out quickly and the gambit stays playable.

1.h4 f5 2.e4.strategy: A pawn offer that opens the diagonal for the queen towards h5, aimed at the kingside Black has just loosened. If Black takes the pawn, White has to make the open lines count, since it is a pawn down with little else going for it.

1.h4 f5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and takes e5 and g5 under control, so White gets on with the game without needless risk. Black's early f-pawn move has loosened the king's side a little, and quiet development is enough to make use of it.

1.h4 f5 2.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre and frees the c1-bishop, giving White a sound queen's pawn game in which the h-pawn move is a spare step. Black's f-pawn move has loosened the kingside and helps little with the rest of the centre.

1.h4 f5 2.e4 fxe4.strategy: Accepts the pawn: Black wins material and removes White's e-pawn from the centre. The kingside is a little loosened by the f-pawn leaving, so Black should watch the open diagonal toward h5, but the extra pawn is sound.

1.h4 f5 2.e4 Nf6.strategy: Declines the gambit, but 3.e5 attacks the knight at once and gains space with tempo. Black has nothing to show for the pawn that was on offer and stands clearly worse, so taking the pawn is much better.

1.h4 f5 2.e4 d6.strategy: Declines the pawn and sets up a solid pawn structure that opens the c8-bishop. If White takes on f5, the bishop recaptures and the offer is returned, leaving Black a level, harmless game.

1.h4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.d3.name: Kádas Opening: Steinbok Gambit
1.h4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.d3.strategy: Hits e4 and opens the c1-bishop, so White presses on with the gambit and plays for rapid development. If Black captures on d3, White recaptures with a lead in development and open lines: still a pawn down, but with real play and a balanced game.

1.h4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e4 pawn, so the gambit pawn is regained unless Black defends it. White keeps the initiative and builds quickly, which is the point of the gambit, while Black has to look after e4 with accurate moves.

1.h4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Qe2.strategy: Attacks the extra pawn with the queen, but blocks the king's bishop and Black simply defends e4 with a developing move or a central pawn. White has spent a tempo, has no lead in development and stays a pawn down for nothing.
